text: Shebang purpose → picks the interpreter → `#!/usr/bin/env bash` finds bash in `PATH`
title: Bash Basics

text: `$@` vs `$*` → `"$@"` keeps each arg separate, `"$*"` glues them into one string
title: Bash Basics

text: Why is `cd` a builtin → a separate program can't change your shell's directory
title: Bash Basics

text: `a=5; a+=2` gives `52` → variables are strings → use `$(( ))` for math
title: Bash Basics

text: `[` vs `[[` → `[` is a command with word splitting, `[[` is a keyword without it
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: `a && b || c` → `c` also runs if `b` fails → not a real if/else
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: `return` vs `exit` → `return` ends the function, `exit` ends the whole script
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: Why never `for f in $(ls)` → filenames with spaces split → use `for f in *`
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: `set -euo pipefail` flag by flag → `-e` stop on failure, `-u` error on unset var, `-o pipefail` pipe fails if any part fails
title: Script Safety

text: Does `set -e` catch everything → no, not inside `if` or before `&&` `||` → safety net, not guarantee
title: Script Safety

text: `trap cleanup EXIT` → cleanup runs even when the script fails
title: Script Safety

text: Common bash pitfalls → quote vars, globs not `ls`, handle failures
title: Script Safety

text: What does the docker CLI do? → nothing by itself; it sends REST API requests to dockerd over /var/run/docker.sock
title: Architecture

text: Why is access to docker.sock dangerous? → whoever can write to it controls dockerd, which runs as root, so it is effectively root access
title: Architecture

text: dockerd vs containerd? → dockerd handles Docker features (API, builds, networks, volumes, logs); containerd only manages images and container lifecycle
title: Architecture

text: What does runc do? → creates namespaces and cgroups, sets the root filesystem, starts the process, then exits
title: Architecture

text: Why a shim per container? → it stays as the container's parent, keeps its logs and exit code, so dockerd/containerd can restart without killing containers
title: Architecture

text: Does Kubernetes need Docker? → no, it talks to containerd directly
title: Architecture

text: What is a daemon? → a background program that runs all the time waiting for work, usually named with a trailing d
title: Architecture

text: Why does a container exit immediately? → its main process ended; e.g. bash with no terminal exits at once
title: Containers

text: docker stop vs docker kill? → stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10s, then SIGKILL; kill sends SIGKILL immediately
title: Containers

text: Is a stopped container deleted? → no, it stays with its writable layer until docker rm
title: Containers

text: What does --rm do? → deletes the container automatically when it stops; it does not remove a running container
title: Containers

text: docker run vs docker start? → run creates a new container; start restarts an existing stopped one
title: Containers

text: docker run vs docker exec? → run makes a new container; exec runs a command inside an existing running one
title: Containers

text: docker ps -aq? → IDs of all containers, running and stopped, used with $( ) to feed other commands
title: Containers

text: docker rm vs docker rmi? → rm removes containers, rmi removes images
title: Containers

text: Exit code 143? → the process got SIGTERM
title: Containers

text: What is the Docker socket? → `/var/run/docker.sock`, the Unix socket the daemon listens on. The CLI and tools like Portainer use the REST API through it
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why is mounting it dangerous? → the daemon runs as root, so a process with the socket can start a container with the host's `/` mounted. It is root on the host
title: The Docker Socket

text: Does `--network none` protect a container that has the socket? → no, the socket is a file mount, not a network path
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why do CI runners mount it? → to start sibling containers on the host's daemon (Docker-out-of-Docker). Docker-in-Docker runs its own daemon in a privileged container instead
title: The Docker Socket

text: How do you make socket access safer? → rootless Docker or Podman, a socket proxy that allows only certain API calls, no mount into untrusted containers
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why is `docker` group membership a security concern? → it can reach the socket, which is equivalent to root
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why is exposing the daemon on TCP `2375` bad? → no TLS or auth, anyone on the network gets root. If you need remote access use `2376` with TLS
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why did Portainer show 0 containers on a newer Docker? → the daemon raised its minimum API version and an old Portainer client was rejected, so upgrade Portainer
title: The Docker Socket

text: Which two mounts does a Portainer container need and why? → the socket (bind mount, to control Docker) and a volume on `/data` (to keep its settings)
title: The Docker Socket

text: Dockerfile vs image vs container? → the Dockerfile is the instructions, the image is what they build, a container is a running instance of the image
title: Dockerfile

text: `RUN` vs `CMD`? → `RUN` executes at build time and saves a layer, `CMD` is stored in the image and executes each time a container starts
title: Dockerfile

text: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`? → `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed executable, `CMD` supplies default arguments and is easy to override with `docker run`
title: Dockerfile

text: `ARG` vs `ENV`? → `ARG` exists only during the build, `ENV` is also set in running containers
title: Dockerfile

text: Why does `docker run --build-arg` fail? → `--build-arg` is a `docker build` option, `ARG` values are fixed once the image is built
title: Dockerfile

text: Why does nginx need `daemon off;`? → a container stops when its main process exits, and nginx backgrounds itself by default
title: Dockerfile

text: Exec form vs shell form of `CMD`? → exec form runs the program directly as the main process, shell form wraps it in `/bin/sh -c`
title: Dockerfile

text: Does `EXPOSE` publish a port? → no, it only documents it, `-p` publishes it
title: Dockerfile

text: `COPY` vs `ADD`? → `ADD` also extracts archives and downloads URLs, `COPY` is simpler and preferred
title: Dockerfile

text: What does `.dockerignore` do? → keeps files like `.git` and `.env` out of the build context so they are not sent to the daemon or copied in
title: Dockerfile

text: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`? → `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed executable, `CMD` is the default command or arguments and is replaced by anything after the image name in `docker run`
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Both in one Dockerfile? → `CMD` is passed as arguments to `ENTRYPOINT`, so the image behaves like a command with default flags
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: How do you override `ENTRYPOINT`? → `docker run --entrypoint cmd image`, in Kubernetes the `command` field
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Why use exec form? → the program is PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` from `docker stop`, shell form puts `/bin/sh -c` in front and the signal may never reach the app
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: A container starts and exits immediately, why? → its main process finished or ran in the background, keep it in the foreground, for nginx `daemon off;`
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: `docker run app ping host` fails on an image with `ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]`, why? → the extra `ping` is appended as an argument and read as a hostname
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Where are `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` visible? → `docker inspect` shows `Path`, `Args`, `Config.Entrypoint` and `Config.Cmd`
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Does `EXPOSE` publish a port? → no, it documents it, `-p` publishes, `-P` publishes all `EXPOSE`d ports to random host ports
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: `EXPOSE 80` and `-p 8000:8000`, what happens? → `-p` wins, host 8000 goes to container 8000, if the app listens on 80 the connection fails with no warning
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: `COPY` vs `ADD`? → `ADD` also extracts local tarballs and downloads URLs, a downloaded archive is not extracted, use `COPY` and `RUN curl` instead
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Why `WORKDIR` instead of `RUN cd`? → `cd` lasts one `RUN`, `WORKDIR` applies to every later instruction and to the running container
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Why run as non-root? → a breakout or a bug then gives an unprivileged user, not root
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Build fails with `Permission denied` in `apt`, why? → `USER` was set before the install, root-only steps must run first
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Can a non-root user run nginx on port 80? → not by default, ports below 1024 need root or a capability, use 8080
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: How do you build with a differently named Dockerfile? → `docker build -f name -t tag .`, the `.` stays the context
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Why are secrets in `ENV` bad? → they are baked into the image layers and show up in `docker inspect` and `docker history`
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: What is an image layer? → a read-only filesystem diff made by an instruction like `RUN` or `COPY`, stacked to form the image and shared between images
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Which instructions make the image bigger? → `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`. `ENV`, `ARG`, `LABEL`, `CMD` are 0B metadata
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: How does the build cache work? → a layer is reused if its instruction and all earlier layers are unchanged. The first change invalidates everything below it
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: How do you order a Dockerfile for fast rebuilds? → rarely changing steps first (base, packages, dependencies), frequently changing steps (your code) last
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Does deleting a file in a later layer reduce image size? → no, the earlier layer still holds it. Delete in the same `RUN`
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Image ID vs tag? → the ID identifies the image content, a tag is a movable name. Rebuilding under the same tag moves the tag to a new ID
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What is a dangling image and how do you remove it? → an untagged image left behind when a tag moves. `docker image prune`
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What does `docker system prune` remove? → stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and unused build cache
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Why are secrets in `ENV` bad, and what do you do instead? → they are stored in the image and visible via `docker history` and `docker inspect`. Pass them at run time or use an IAM role, and rotate any key that was baked in
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What does `<missing>` mean in `docker history`? → those layers have no local image ID, which is normal for layers from a base image or BuildKit
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What is an image layer? → a read-only slice of the filesystem created by RUN, COPY or ADD, identified by a content hash
title: Images & Storage

text: What is copy-on-write? → changing a file from a lower layer copies it up into the container's writable layer first; the image is never modified
title: Images & Storage

text: Why doesn't deleting a file in a later layer shrink the image? → it only adds a whiteout marker; the file still exists in the earlier layer
title: Images & Storage

text: Does latest mean newest? → no, it is just a default tag name that can point anywhere
title: Images & Storage

text: docker pull says manifest unknown for :latest? → the repo has no latest tag; pass an existing tag explicitly
title: Images & Storage

text: Tag vs digest? → tag is mutable, digest (sha256) always points to the exact same image
title: Images & Storage

text: RUN vs CMD? → RUN executes at build time; CMD is the default command each time a container starts
title: Images & Storage

text: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? → ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can replace
title: Images & Storage

text: Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it; only -p publishes
title: Images & Storage

text: Why order Dockerfile instructions carefully? → a changed layer invalidates the cache for every layer after it
title: Images & Storage

text: Volume vs bind mount? → volume is managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes; bind mount maps a host path I choose
title: Images & Storage

text: Where does container data go when the container is removed? → the writable layer is deleted; only volumes and bind mounts survive
title: Images & Storage

text: How do you check how Docker was installed on Ubuntu? → dpkg -l for docker-ce vs docker.io, and snap list
title: Install & Upgrade

text: docker.io vs docker-ce? → docker.io is Ubuntu's package and lags behind; docker-ce comes from Docker's official repo
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Service shows disabled but Docker works? → socket activation: systemd starts dockerd when something connects to docker.socket
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Why is docker0 missing? → dockerd isn't running (or bridge is disabled in daemon.json); dockerd creates docker0 at startup
title: Install & Upgrade

text: enable vs start? → start runs it now, enable starts it at boot; enable --now does both
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Does removing docker.io delete my images? → no, apt remove without --purge keeps /var/lib/docker
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Container vs VM? → VM has its own kernel and full OS; container is a process sharing the host kernel, so it is smaller and starts in milliseconds but isolation is weaker
title: Introduction

text: What is a container, technically? → a normal Linux process with namespaces (what it sees), cgroups (what it uses) and a layered filesystem
title: Introduction

text: Why does a container stop when its app exits? → the container lives only as long as its main process (PID 1)
title: Introduction

text: Exit code 137? → process got SIGKILL, often the OOM killer after hitting the memory limit
title: Introduction

text: Can a Linux container run on a Windows kernel natively? → no, containers share the host kernel; Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM for this
title: Introduction

text: Image vs container? → image is the read-only template, container is a running instance of it with its own writable layer
title: Introduction

text: Where does docker logs get its data? → from /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log, written by the json-file log driver
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: How do you find a container's log file path? → docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}' <name>
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: Why do nginx notices appear as stderr? → nginx writes its own logs to stderr by design; it does not mean an error
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: What happens to logs when a container is removed? → the whole container folder, logs included, is deleted
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: How do you stop container logs filling the disk? → set log-opts max-size and max-file in /etc/docker/daemon.json
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: Where does a container's /etc/hostname, /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf come from? → files in its folder under /var/lib/docker/containers, mounted in at start
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: What is a multi-stage build? → several `FROM` stages in one Dockerfile, a heavy stage compiles the app and the last, slim stage copies only the artifact with `COPY --from`
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Why use it? → the final image has no compiler, source or build cache, so it is smaller and has a smaller attack surface
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: What is a distroless image? → a base with the app runtime only, no shell, no package manager, no OS tools
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Benefits of distroless? → fewer CVEs, smaller image, an attacker who gets in has no shell or `curl` to use
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Downsides? → no `docker exec` shell, no `RUN apt install` in the final stage, only exec-form `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`, debugging needs the `:debug` tag or an ephemeral container
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Why did `RUN apt update` fail on a distroless base? → `RUN` starts `/bin/sh -c` and the image has no `/bin/sh`
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: How do you debug a distroless container in Kubernetes? → `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container that shares the pod's namespaces
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: `distroless` vs `scratch` vs `alpine`? → `scratch` is empty and only fits static binaries, distroless adds CA certs, timezone data and a non-root user, `alpine` is small but has a shell and uses musl
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: How do you harden an image? → multi-stage build, minimal or distroless base, non-root `USER`, pinned versions, no secrets in `ENV`
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: What does `docker build --target` do? → builds only up to the named stage and tags that
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: What is a Linux namespace? → a kernel feature that gives a set of processes its own view of a resource (processes, network, mounts, hostname...)
title: Namespaces

text: Namespaces vs cgroups? → namespaces limit what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can use
title: Namespaces

text: Name the 7 namespaces → PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP (plus TIME on newer kernels)
title: Namespaces

text: Is container root the same as host root? → by default yes; user namespace remapping or rootless Docker changes that
title: Namespaces

text: How do you get a shell in a container's network namespace from the host? → nsenter -t <pid> -n
title: Namespaces

text: Why can 10 containers all listen on port 80? → each has its own network namespace
title: Namespaces

text: What is docker0? → a Linux bridge (software switch) created by dockerd; containers plug into it via veth pairs and use 172.17.0.1 as their gateway
title: Networking

text: What is a veth pair? → a virtual cable; one end is eth0 inside the container, the other is plugged into the bridge on the host
title: Networking

text: What does -p 8080:80 mean? → host port 8080 forwards to container port 80 (HOST:CONTAINER) via an iptables DNAT rule
title: Networking

text: Why can't I reach a container without -p? → its IP is private to the host; nothing listens on the host port
title: Networking

text: Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it
title: Networking

text: How does a container reach the internet? → through docker0, then iptables MASQUERADE rewrites its source IP to the host's
title: Networking

text: Why can two containers use port 80 but not the same host port? → each has its own network namespace, but the host has only one of each port
title: Networking

text: Default bridge vs user-defined network? → user-defined networks have built-in DNS so containers reach each other by name
title: Networking

text: Why does a published port ignore UFW? → Docker's iptables rules are evaluated before UFW's
title: Networking

text: What is a network driver? → the type of network, i.e. how Docker wires the container: bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan/ipvlan
title: Networking

text: Can a container on one user-defined network reach a container on another? → no, bridges are isolated by iptables; connect the container to both networks to cross
title: Networking

text: How do you add a running container to another network? → docker network connect <network> <container>; it gets a second interface (eth1)
title: Networking

text: Which DNS server do containers on a user-defined network use? → Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11
title: Networking

text: Why use names instead of container IPs? → IPs change when containers restart, names stay the same
title: Networking

text: When would you use --network host? → when the container must see or serve on the host's network directly, e.g. Node Exporter; you lose isolation and can get port conflicts
title: Networking

text: Why does docker ps show no ports in host mode? → nothing is forwarded; the app listens on the host's port directly
title: Networking

text: Why does a /16 network show 65530 available IPs with 3 containers? → 65,536 minus the network address, gateway, broadcast and the 3 containers
title: Networking

text: Registry vs repository vs tag? → a registry is the server, a repository is one image's set of versions, a tag is one version
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: What does docker pull ubuntu actually pull? → docker.io/library/ubuntu:latest
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: Does latest mean the newest version? → no, it is just the default tag name; pin explicit tags or digests in production
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: Tag vs digest? → a tag is a movable label; a digest is the sha256 of the content and never changes
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: Why does docker push my-first-image fail on Docker Hub? → the image name needs your namespace, e.g. username/my-first-image
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: What does docker tag do? → adds another name to the same image ID, nothing is copied
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: How do you push to ECR? → get a token with aws ecr get-login-password, docker login to the account's registry URL, tag with the full ECR name, push
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: What is the build context? → the folder sent to the daemon during docker build; COPY and ADD only see files inside it, and .dockerignore trims it
title: Registries & Pushing Images

text: Volume vs bind mount? → a volume is managed by Docker and referenced by name, a bind mount maps a host path you choose. Volumes for persistent app data, bind mounts for dev code and config
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Container was deleted and the data is gone, why? → the data was in the container's writable layer. Mount a volume on the data path
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Does `--rm` delete a named volume? → no, only the container (and anonymous volumes). Named volumes stay until `docker volume rm`
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: How do you tell `-v` volume from bind mount? → source starting with `/` or `./` is a bind mount, a plain name is a volume
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Why prefer `--mount` over `-v`? → it is explicit, and it errors on a missing bind source instead of creating an empty directory
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Files written by a container show up root-owned on the host? → the container runs as root. Use `--user` with the host UID and GID
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Where are named volumes stored on Linux? → `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data`, readable only by root
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: How would you back up a volume? → run a throwaway container that mounts the volume and a host folder, and `tar` the data
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: When would you use `tmpfs`? → temporary or sensitive data you don't want written to disk
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: When does a deferred call run? → just before the surrounding function returns, on every exit path including panics
title: Defer

text: When are a deferred call's arguments evaluated? → immediately, when the defer statement executes; only the call is delayed
title: Defer

text: In what order do multiple defers run? → last in, first out, like a stack
title: Defer

text: Why is LIFO the right order for defers? → resources are released in reverse of how they were acquired
title: Defer

text: What is the classic use of defer? → cleanup such as closing files and response bodies or unlocking mutexes
title: Defer

text: Why is defer inside a long loop risky? → deferred calls pile up until the function returns, holding resources open
title: Defer

text: Why check err before deferring Close? → if the open failed the value may be nil and the deferred Close would fail or panic
title: Defer

text: What are the parts of a Go source file? → package clause, imports, then top-level declarations (func, const, var, type)
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: Why does Go fail on unused imports and variables? → to keep code clean and builds fast; unused code is treated as a likely mistake
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: go run vs go build? → go run compiles to a temporary binary and runs it; go build writes the binary to disk
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: Why is Go popular for DevOps tools? → it builds single static binaries with no runtime dependencies, easy to ship and cross-compile
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: How do you read a Go compile error location? → file:line:column, and fix the first error since later ones are often knock-on
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: What are the rules for a Go test? → file ends in _test.go, function starts with Test and takes *testing.T, run with go test
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: What does t.Errorf do? → reports a failure with a formatted message and lets the test continue
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: gofmt vs go vet vs golangci-lint? → gofmt formats, go vet runs built-in correctness checks, golangci-lint runs many linters including vet in one pass
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: What does errcheck catch? → returned errors that the code ignores
title: Go Files, Running & Testing

text: How does Go handle errors without exceptions? → functions return an error as their last value and the caller checks if err != nil
title: Functions & Printing

text: What is the blank identifier? → _ , used to discard a value you must receive but don't need
title: Functions & Printing

text: What are named return values? → result parameters declared with names; they start at zero values and a bare return sends them back
title: Functions & Printing

text: When should you avoid naked returns? → in long functions, because the reader can't tell what is being returned
title: Functions & Printing

text: Println vs Printf? → Println prints values separated by spaces with a newline; Printf uses a format string with verbs and adds nothing
title: Functions & Printing

text: Why use %q in test failure messages? → it quotes strings, so empty strings and stray spaces become visible
title: Functions & Printing

text: How do you find a value's type at runtime while debugging? → fmt.Printf("%T", v)
title: Functions & Printing

text: Is math/rand part of the math package? → no, it is a separate package stored under the math/ directory
title: Functions & Printing

text: GOROOT vs GOPATH? → GOROOT is where Go is installed; GOPATH (default ~/go) holds installed binaries and the module cache
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: Does your code need to live in GOPATH? → no, since modules your project can be anywhere; go.mod marks the project root
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: Where does go install put binaries? → GOBIN, which defaults to $GOPATH/bin
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: What is the module cache? → $GOPATH/pkg/mod, read-only copies of downloaded modules stored by path and version
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: What is GOCACHE? → the build cache of compiled packages and test results that makes rebuilds fast
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: Setting precedence in Go? → environment variables override go env -w settings, which override the go.env defaults
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: How do you force tests to re-run? → go test -count=1 or go clean -testcache
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: Why are module names URLs? → the path tells Go where to fetch the code from
title: GOPATH, Caches & go env

text: What is GOROOT? → the directory where Go itself is installed, holding the go command, compiler and linker, and the standard library source
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: What does go build actually run? → the compile tool for each package, then the link tool to produce one binary
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: How does the shell decide which go binary runs? → it searches the PATH directories in order and runs the first match; which go shows it
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: What is GOPROXY? → where Go downloads modules from; default is the proxy.golang.org mirror with direct as fallback
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: What does GOSUMDB do? → verifies downloaded modules against a public checksum database so tampered code is rejected
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: What does GOTOOLCHAIN=auto do? → downloads and uses a newer Go toolchain when a module's go.mod requires one
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: Why is having two Go installs a problem? → different tools can pick different versions, giving inconsistent builds and confusing errors
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: Why run hash -r? → bash caches command locations; after moving or removing a binary it clears that cache
title: Installation & GOROOT

text: How many loop keywords does Go have? → one, for; while and infinite loops are written with for
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: How do you write a while loop in Go? → for condition { }
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: Where is a variable declared in a for init statement visible? → only inside that for statement
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: What is an if short statement? → a statement before the condition, like if v := f(); v < 10, whose variables exist only in the if and its else
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: Why use the if short statement for err? → it keeps err scoped to one check so it can't leak or clash with later errors
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: How does Go's switch differ from C's? → only the matching case runs with no break needed, and cases need not be constants or integers
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: What does fallthrough do? → forces execution to continue into the next case
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: In what order are switch cases evaluated? → top to bottom, stopping at the first match; later cases are not evaluated
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: What is a switch with no condition? → the same as switch true; each case is a boolean expression, used to replace long if-else chains
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: Are function arguments evaluated before the call? → yes, all arguments are fully computed before the function body runs
title: Loops & Conditionals

text: Module vs package in Go? → a module is a versioned project defined by go.mod; a package is one directory of .go files inside it
title: Modules & Packages

text: What does go mod init do? → creates go.mod with the module path and the Go version, marking the directory as a module root
title: Modules & Packages

text: What is go.sum for? → it records checksums of dependency versions so builds verify they get exactly the same code
title: Modules & Packages

text: How does Go find the module for a nested folder? → it walks up the directory tree to the nearest go.mod
title: Modules & Packages

text: What makes a Go program executable? → a package named main with a func main, the entry point
title: Modules & Packages

text: Can one directory hold two main functions? → no, a directory is one package; separate programs go in separate directories such as cmd/<name>
title: Modules & Packages

text: How is an import path for your own package formed? → module path from go.mod plus the package's directory path
title: Modules & Packages

text: How does Go control visibility? → identifiers starting with a capital letter are exported, lowercase ones are package-private
title: Modules & Packages

text: Why do real module paths look like URLs? → so go get can locate and download the code, e.g. github.com/user/repo
title: Modules & Packages

text: What is a zero value in Go? → the value a variable gets when declared without one: 0, false, "" or nil depending on the type
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: Why does Go have zero values instead of undefined? → every variable always holds a valid, predictable value, so there is no uninitialized memory to read
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: var vs := ? → := declares and infers inside functions only; var works everywhere and can declare without a value
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: When does := fail on an existing name? → when no variable on the left side is new
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: How does type inference work for literals? → 42 becomes int, 4.2 float64, "x" string, true bool
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: Does Go convert int to float64 automatically? → no, conversions are always explicit with T(v)
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: What happens when converting a float variable to int? → the fraction is truncated toward zero
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: Why is string(65) not "65"? → it converts the number to the character with that code point; use strconv.Itoa for decimal text
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: What is an untyped constant? → a constant with no fixed type that takes the type required where it is used, kept at high precision until then
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: Can a constant be declared with := ? → no, constants use const name = value
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: What are byte and rune? → aliases for uint8 and int32, used for raw bytes and Unicode characters
title: Variables, Types & Constants

text: Who created Go and when? → Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson at Google, started in 2007, open-sourced in 2009, Go 1.0 in 2012
title: What is Go

text: Why was Go created? → slow C++ builds, overly complex languages, and the need for easy concurrency on multicore networked servers at Google scale
title: What is Go

text: Is Go compiled or interpreted? → compiled to native machine code
title: What is Go

text: Why is Go popular for DevOps and cloud tools? → single static binaries, fast startup, low memory use, strong networking stdlib and built-in concurrency
title: What is Go

text: Why does a Go binary run on a server without Go installed? → the runtime and dependencies are linked into the binary
title: What is Go

text: What is a goroutine? → a lightweight function running concurrently, managed by the Go runtime rather than the OS, with a small growable stack
title: What is Go

text: What is the Go 1 compatibility promise? → programs written for Go 1 continue to compile and run on later Go 1.x releases
title: What is Go

text: How does Go handle errors without exceptions? → functions return an error value that the caller checks with if err != nil
title: What is Go

text: Does Go support object-oriented programming? → partly: structs with methods and interfaces, but no classes or inheritance; it favours composition
title: What is Go

text: When were generics added to Go? → Go 1.18, in 2022
title: What is Go

text: Name tools written in Go → Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus, etcd, Helm, Vault
title: What is Go

text: Go vs Python for infra tooling? → Go is faster, typed and ships as one binary; Python is quicker for small scripts and data work
title: What is Go

text: Components of the control plane? → kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, and cloud-controller-manager on cloud clusters
title: Architecture

text: Components of a worker node? → kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime (containerd/CRI-O), plus CNI and CSI plugins
title: Architecture

text: What does the API server do? → authenticates, authorizes, runs admission, validates and stores objects in etcd, and lets other components watch for changes; it is the only component that talks to etcd
title: Architecture

text: Does the scheduler start Pods? → no, it only writes the chosen nodeName into the Pod; the kubelet on that node starts it
title: Architecture

text: How does the scheduler pick a node? → filter out nodes that can't run the Pod, score the rest, reserve and bind the best one
title: Architecture

text: What happens if the control plane goes down? → running Pods keep running, but nothing can be created, changed or rescheduled until it is back
title: Architecture

text: Does kube-proxy assign Pod IPs? → no, the CNI plugin does; kube-proxy programs iptables/IPVS/nftables rules so Service IPs reach healthy Pods
title: Architecture

text: Is the kubelet a Pod? → no, it runs as a systemd service on each node
title: Architecture

text: CRI vs CNI vs CSI? → CRI is how the kubelet talks to the container runtime, CNI gives Pods networking, CSI gives Pods storage
title: Architecture

text: What is the cloud-controller-manager? → the control-plane piece that talks to the cloud provider's API, e.g. creating load balancers for LoadBalancer Services
title: Architecture

text: What is a container, technically? → a normal Linux process isolated with namespaces, limited with cgroups, running on its own root filesystem
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Namespaces vs cgroups? → namespaces isolate what a process can see; cgroups limit and measure what it can use
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Which namespace do containers in a Pod share? → the network namespace, held by the pause container, so they share one IP and use localhost
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Container exceeds its CPU limit vs its memory limit? → CPU gets throttled; memory gets OOMKilled with exit code 137
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Requests vs limits? → requests are used by the scheduler to place the Pod; limits are enforced on the node through cgroups
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: What is runc? → the low-level OCI runtime that containerd calls to create the container; it sets up namespaces and cgroups, starts the process and exits
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: What is containerd? → a CNCF high-level runtime that pulls and stores images, manages container lifecycle and calls runc; Kubernetes talks to it over CRI
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Why did Kubernetes drop Docker? → Docker doesn't implement CRI, so Kubernetes needed the dockershim adapter; it was removed in 1.24 in favour of containerd and CRI-O
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Do Docker-built images still work on Kubernetes? → yes, they are OCI images
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: What keeps a container running if containerd restarts? → the containerd-shim, which is the container's parent process
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: Why are containers weaker isolation than VMs? → they share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape; gVisor and Kata add a stronger boundary
title: Container Runtime Internals

text: A Pod can't resolve a Service name, how do you debug? → confirm the Service exists in that namespace, curl the ClusterIP to separate DNS from Service problems, check resolv.conf, check that CoreDNS Pods are Ready and read their logs
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: CoreDNS Pods show 0/1 Running, what does that mean? → the process runs but fails its readiness probe, so the kube-dns Service has no endpoints and DNS queries go unanswered
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: CoreDNS logs say plugin kubernetes not ready, why? → CoreDNS can't sync with the API server, often because kube-proxy rules for the kubernetes Service ClusterIP are missing on that node
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: How do you see why a container keeps crashing? → kubectl logs <pod> --previous shows the last crashed run
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: Why can kube-proxy crash with too many open files on kind? → kind nodes share the host kernel, and the default inotify instance limit is exhausted; raise fs.inotify limits with sysctl
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: Is it safe to delete a kube-proxy Pod? → yes, it's a DaemonSet Pod and is recreated immediately on the same node
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: Service Endpoints are filled but connections are refused? → targetPort doesn't match the port the app listens on
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: Service Endpoints are empty? → selector doesn't match Pod labels, Pods aren't Ready, or they're in another namespace
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: General debugging approach? → reproduce the exact error, split the path in half with tests, check get/describe/logs, compare healthy vs broken, go one layer down, fix, verify and document
title: Debugging Services & DNS

text: Walk me through what happens on kubectl apply of a Deployment → kubectl sends it to the API server, which authenticates, authorizes, runs admission and stores it in etcd; the Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects; the scheduler assigns each Pod a node; the kubelet on that node asks containerd to pull the image and start the containers, CNI gives the Pod an IP, and the kubelet reports status back
title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod

text: When kubectl says "deployment created", is anything running? → no, only the object is stored in etcd; controllers, the scheduler and the kubelet do the rest asynchronously
title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod

text: Who recreates a deleted Pod, the Deployment or the ReplicaSet? → the ReplicaSet controller; the Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets
title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod

text: Do controllers read etcd directly? → no, everything goes through the API server, which is the only component talking to etcd
title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod

text: A Pod is stuck in Pending, what do you check? → kubectl describe pod and its Events, usually the scheduler couldn't find a node because of resources, taints or affinity
title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod

text: CrashLoopBackOff, what do you check? → kubectl logs --previous for the crashed container, then the command, config and probes
title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod

text: What is etcd? → a distributed, consistent key-value store that holds all Kubernetes cluster state; only the API server talks to it
title: etcd & Raft

text: What happens if you lose etcd with no backup? → the cluster loses its record of what should exist; you restore from an etcd snapshot
title: etcd & Raft

text: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted? → not by default; they are base64-encoded in etcd, so you enable encryption at rest (ideally with KMS) and restrict etcd access
title: etcd & Raft

text: What is Raft? → a consensus algorithm: one elected leader takes writes and replicates them, a write commits once a majority acknowledges it, and followers elect a new leader if the leader fails
title: etcd & Raft

text: What is quorum and why odd numbers? → a majority, N/2+1; 4 members tolerate the same single failure as 3, so even numbers add cost without extra safety
title: etcd & Raft

text: What happens when etcd loses quorum? → it stops accepting writes, so the Kubernetes API can't make changes; existing Pods keep running
title: etcd & Raft

text: How does Raft prevent split-brain? → only a side with a majority can elect a leader and commit writes, so two leaders can never both write
title: etcd & Raft

text: What is the WAL? → the write-ahead log: every change is logged to disk before being applied, so etcd can replay it after a crash
title: etcd & Raft

text: Are imperative commands used in production? → not to manage workloads; production uses declarative manifests in Git applied by CI/CD or GitOps, while imperative commands are used to generate manifests and for debugging
title: Imperative Commands

text: --dry-run=client vs --dry-run=server? → client builds the object locally without creating it; server sends it to the API server for schema and admission validation but does not persist it
title: Imperative Commands

text: Does containerPort open or expose a port? → no, it is informational; the application decides which port it listens on and a Service exposes it, though kubectl expose and named ports use it
title: Imperative Commands

text: Why must the Deployment exist before kubectl expose, even with a client dry-run? → expose reads the live Deployment to copy its selector into the Service
title: Imperative Commands

text: How do you set a fixed nodePort when kubectl expose has no flag for it? → generate the YAML and add nodePort under ports, or use kubectl create service nodeport --node-port and fix its selector
title: Imperative Commands

text: Why put --- between objects in one file? → it separates YAML documents; without it the objects merge into one document with duplicate keys
title: Imperative Commands

text: How do you test a ClusterIP Service? → from a temporary Pod inside the cluster, e.g. kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- wget -qO- svc:port
title: Imperative Commands

text: How does a Pod resolve a short Service name? → /etc/resolv.conf points to the kube-dns Service (CoreDNS) and its search domains expand the name to service.namespace.svc.cluster.local
title: Imperative Commands

text: What does ndots:5 do and why can it hurt? → names with fewer than five dots try the search domains first, so external names cause several failed lookups before the real one
title: Imperative Commands

text: What happens if you change a Pod's label so it no longer matches? → it drops out of the Service endpoints and the ReplicaSet creates a replacement, leaving the relabelled Pod orphaned
title: Imperative Commands

text: What is kind? → a tool that runs Kubernetes clusters locally, with each node as a Docker container; used for learning, testing and CI
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: Why create a kind cluster from a config file? → version control, reproducible and declarative setup, shareable across the team, single source of truth
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: Must kubectl match the cluster version exactly? → no, kubectl is supported within one minor version of the API server
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: What is a kubeconfig? → kubectl's config file, ~/.kube/config by default, with clusters (API server + CA), users (credentials) and contexts that pair a cluster with a user and namespace; current-context decides where kubectl points
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: What is a context? → a saved combination of cluster, user and namespace
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: use-context vs set-context? → use-context switches the current context; set-context edits a context, e.g. its default namespace
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: Does the kubeconfig change when you create a Deployment? → no, only when clusters or contexts change; workloads live in etcd inside the cluster
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: Why is the kubeconfig sensitive? → it holds credentials; whoever has it has your access to the cluster
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: How do you avoid running a command on the wrong cluster? → check current-context before acting, use clear context names, or pass --context explicitly
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: Kubernetes namespace vs Linux namespace? → a Kubernetes namespace groups API objects logically; a Linux namespace isolates what a process can see
title: kind, kubeconfig & Contexts

text: What is manual scheduling? → setting spec.nodeName in the Pod manifest so the Pod is bound to a node directly and the scheduler is skipped
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: Why can a Pod with nodeName run on a tainted control-plane node? → NoSchedule taints are enforced by the scheduler, and nodeName bypasses the scheduler; the kubelet doesn't check them
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: Does nodeName bypass NoExecute taints? → no, NoExecute is enforced after the Pod is running and the Pod gets evicted
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: What happens if nodeName points to a node without enough resources? → the kubelet rejects the Pod on admission and it fails with OutOfcpu or OutOfmemory
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: What happens if nodeName points to a node that doesn't exist? → the Pod stays Pending because no kubelet claims it, and the Pod garbage collector deletes it
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: What is the proper way to run a Pod on a specific node? → nodeSelector or node affinity, plus a toleration if the node is tainted, so the scheduler still checks the rules
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: How do control-plane components run on a kubeadm cluster? → as static Pods from manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests on the control-plane node
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: What is a static Pod? → a Pod managed directly by the kubelet of one node from a local manifest file, without the API server or scheduler
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: How do you find the static Pod directory? → the staticPodPath field in the kubelet config, usually /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: What is a mirror Pod? → a read-only object the kubelet creates in the API server so a static Pod shows in kubectl, named pod-name dash node-name
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: Why does kubectl delete not remove a static Pod? → it only deletes the mirror Pod; the kubelet still has the manifest and recreates it
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: How do you delete a static Pod? → remove its manifest file from the static Pod directory on that node
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: Static Pod vs DaemonSet? → a static Pod is managed by one node's kubelet from a file and needs no API server; a DaemonSet is managed by a controller through the API server and runs one Pod per node
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: Can you use static Pods on EKS or GKE control planes? → no, the provider manages the control plane and you have no access to its nodes
title: Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

text: What is a namespace in Kubernetes? → a logical partition of one cluster that scopes resource names and is the unit for RBAC, resource quotas and network policies
title: Namespaces

text: Do namespaces provide network isolation? → no, Pods in any namespace can reach each other by default; isolation needs NetworkPolicies enforced by the CNI, plus RBAC and quotas
title: Namespaces

text: How does a Pod reach a Service in another namespace? → service.namespace or service.namespace.svc.cluster.local on the Service port
title: Namespaces

text: Why does the short Service name only work in the same namespace? → the Pod's resolv.conf search list starts with its own namespace.svc.cluster.local
title: Namespaces

text: Which resources are not namespaced? → Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, CRDs and Namespaces themselves
title: Namespaces

text: What are the default namespaces? → default, kube-system, kube-public and kube-node-lease
title: Namespaces

text: What is kube-node-lease for? → it holds a Lease per node that the kubelet renews as a lightweight heartbeat for node health
title: Namespaces

text: What happens when you delete a namespace? → every namespaced object inside it is deleted; it stays Terminating until finalizers complete
title: Namespaces

text: Why is a namespace stuck in Terminating? → a resource inside has a finalizer whose controller can't finish, often a CRD whose operator was removed
title: Namespaces

text: How do you change the default namespace for kubectl? → kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=name, which is saved in the kubeconfig context
title: Namespaces

text: Can a Service select Pods in another namespace? → no, a Service selector only matches Pods in its own namespace
title: Namespaces

text: What do ResourceQuota and LimitRange do? → ResourceQuota caps the total resources and object counts of a namespace; LimitRange sets default and min/max requests and limits per Pod or container
title: Namespaces

text: Namespaces or separate clusters for prod? → namespaces are cheap soft isolation within one control plane; separate clusters give a hard boundary for blast radius, security and upgrades
title: Namespaces

text: Node vs Pod? → a node is a worker machine that provides compute; a Pod is the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers, scheduled onto a node
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: What is a Pod? → the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing a network namespace (one IP) and volumes
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: How do containers in the same Pod talk? → over localhost, because they share the Pod's network namespace
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: What is the pause container? → a tiny container that holds the Pod's network namespace open so app containers can join it
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: What happens if a bare Pod dies? → nothing recreates it; only controllers like ReplicaSets bring Pods back
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: How does a ReplicaSet know which Pods are its own? → by label selector, not by name or owner
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: You create a Pod with the same labels as a ReplicaSet's Pods, what happens? → the ReplicaSet counts it and deletes one Pod to get back to the desired count
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Why use a Deployment instead of a ReplicaSet? → a ReplicaSet can't do rolling updates; a Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet per version and shifts Pods gradually, which also enables rollback
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: How does a rollback work? → the old ReplicaSet is kept at 0 replicas; rollback scales it back up and scales the new one down
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: New image tag doesn't exist, does the app go down? → no, new Pods fail with ImagePullBackOff while old Pods keep running, because old Pods are only removed once new ones are Ready
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: ReplicationController vs ReplicaSet? → same job; RC is legacy core v1 with equality-based selectors only, RS is apps/v1 and also supports set-based selectors, and is what Deployments use
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Equality-based vs set-based selectors? → equality matches exact values (=, !=); set-based uses In, NotIn, Exists and DoesNotExist; rules are ANDed
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Can a cluster run many ReplicaSets? → yes; names must be unique per namespace and selectors shouldn't overlap or they fight over Pods
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: You change the image in a bare ReplicaSet, what happens? → existing Pods keep the old image; only Pods created later use the new one
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: RollingUpdate vs Recreate? → RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually without downtime; Recreate deletes all old Pods first, used when two versions can't run together
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control? → maxSurge is how many extra Pods may exist during an update, maxUnavailable is how many may be unavailable; both default to 25%
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Labels vs annotations? → labels identify objects and are used by selectors; annotations hold non-identifying metadata for humans and tools and are never used for selection
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: How do you record why a revision was made? → set the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation, shown in kubectl rollout history
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Does a rollback restore the old revision number? → no, it creates a new revision with the old template; the old number disappears from history
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: How far back can you roll back? → as far as revisionHistoryLimit allows, 10 old ReplicaSets by default
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Why pause a Deployment? → to batch several changes into one rollout, or to stop a rollout while investigating a problem
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: Why does kubectl warn after rollout undo? → the live object changed but last-applied-configuration didn't, so the next kubectl apply may behave unexpectedly; update the YAML and re-apply
title: Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

text: What is RBAC in Kubernetes? → the authorization layer; Roles and ClusterRoles define allowed verbs on resources, RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings attach them to users, groups or ServiceAccounts
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: Role vs ClusterRole? → a Role is limited to one namespace; a ClusterRole is cluster-wide or reusable across namespaces
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: Can a RoleBinding reference a ClusterRole? → yes, and it grants those permissions only inside the binding's namespace
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: Can you write a deny rule? → no, RBAC is additive; anything not allowed is denied
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: Authentication vs authorization? → authentication proves who you are; authorization (RBAC) decides what you may do
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: Where do users come from? → outside Kubernetes, through certificates or OIDC; ServiceAccounts are the only identities stored as objects
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: How do you check permissions? → kubectl auth can-i, with --as to test another user or ServiceAccount
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: Can you change a binding's roleRef? → no, delete and recreate the binding
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: What is least privilege? → give each identity only the exact verbs and resources it needs, avoiding cluster-admin and wildcards
title: RBAC & Request Flow

text: REST vs gRPC? → REST is resource-oriented, JSON over HTTP, easy to debug and works everywhere, best for public APIs; gRPC is contract-first with protobuf over HTTP/2, faster, strongly typed and has native streaming, best for internal service calls
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: Why is gRPC faster? → binary protobuf payloads are smaller and cheaper to parse, and HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: What is protobuf? → a binary, schema-first serialization format; you define messages in a .proto file and generate typed code, and field numbers replace field names on the wire
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: How does protobuf stay backward compatible? → old code ignores unknown field numbers; never reuse or change a field number, mark removed ones reserved
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: Is protobuf encryption? → no, it is only an encoding format
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: Where does Kubernetes use gRPC? → API server to etcd, and the kubelet to the container runtime (CRI), storage drivers (CSI) and device plugins
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: What protocol does kubectl use? → REST over HTTPS to the API server; -v=8 shows the requests
title: REST, gRPC & Protobuf

text: Why do we need Services? → Pod IPs change on every restart, so a Service gives a stable IP and DNS name and load-balances across the current Ready Pods
title: Services

text: How does a Service know which Pods to send traffic to? → its label selector; the EndpointSlice controller keeps a list of Ready Pods with matching labels in the same namespace
title: Services

text: port vs targetPort vs nodePort? → port is the Service's port that callers use, targetPort is the port the app in the Pod listens on, nodePort is the port opened on every node for outside traffic
title: Services

text: Is the ClusterIP assigned to any interface? → no, it's virtual; kube-proxy programs iptables/IPVS/nftables rules on every node that DNAT it to a Pod IP
title: Services

text: Who does the load balancing for a ClusterIP Service? → kube-proxy's rules in the node kernel, choosing a random endpoint per new connection; no proxy process sits in the data path in iptables mode
title: Services

text: What does CoreDNS do for Services? → watches the API server and answers name lookups, mapping service names to ClusterIPs, or to a CNAME for ExternalName
title: Services

text: Pods are Running but the Service's Endpoints are empty, why? → the selector doesn't match the Pod labels, the Pods aren't Ready, or they're in another namespace
title: Services

text: Endpoints are filled but requests get connection refused? → targetPort doesn't match the port the app actually listens on
title: Services

text: Does a NodePort Service also have a ClusterIP? → yes, NodePort builds on ClusterIP and LoadBalancer builds on NodePort
title: Services

text: Default NodePort range? → 30000–32767
title: Services

text: What happens with NodePort if a node goes down? → clients using that node's IP fail and must switch manually; inside the cluster its Pods are removed from endpoints after the node goes NotReady (~40 s) and replaced after eviction (~5 min)
title: Services

text: externalTrafficPolicy Cluster vs Local? → Cluster forwards to Pods on any node but SNATs and hides the client IP; Local only uses Pods on the receiving node and preserves the client IP
title: Services

text: Who creates the cloud load balancer for a LoadBalancer Service? → the cloud-controller-manager, through the cloud provider's API
title: Services

text: Why is EXTERNAL-IP pending on kind or bare metal? → there's no cloud controller to provision a load balancer; use MetalLB or cloud-provider-kind
title: Services

text: Why not one LoadBalancer per app in production? → cost and no L7 routing; use one LoadBalancer for the ingress controller and ClusterIP Services behind Ingress
title: Services

text: What is an ExternalName Service? → a DNS CNAME alias to an external hostname with no ClusterIP, selector or proxying
title: Services

text: What is a headless Service? → clusterIP: None, DNS returns the individual Pod IPs, used with StatefulSets
title: Services

text: Why does kind need extraPortMappings? → nodes are Docker containers, so the host port must be mapped into a node container to reach a NodePort via localhost; it can only be set at cluster creation
title: Services

text: What are taints and tolerations? → a taint on a node repels Pods; a toleration on a Pod lets it be scheduled onto a node with a matching taint
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: Does a toleration make a Pod run on the tainted node? → no, it only allows it; to attract a Pod to a node use nodeSelector or node affinity
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: What are the three taint effects? → NoSchedule blocks new Pods, PreferNoSchedule avoids the node if possible, NoExecute blocks new Pods and evicts running ones that don't tolerate it
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: What happens to running Pods when a NoSchedule taint is added? → nothing, they keep running; only NoExecute evicts
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: Difference between Equal and Exists? → Equal needs key and value to match; Exists only needs the key and ignores the value
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: What does a toleration with only operator Exists do? → tolerates every taint, which is how DaemonSets run on all nodes
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: What is tolerationSeconds? → for NoExecute taints, how long a Pod may stay on the node after the taint appears before it is evicted
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: Why do Pods have not-ready and unreachable tolerations by default? → the DefaultTolerationSeconds admission plugin adds them with 300 seconds so Pods aren't evicted on a short node outage
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: Why can't normal Pods run on the control plane? → kubeadm taints it with node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule to protect the API server and etcd
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: A node has two taints and the Pod tolerates one, can it schedule there? → no, the Pod must tolerate every taint on the node
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: How do you remove a taint? → kubectl taint nodes node key=value:effect with a trailing dash, or key- to remove all taints with that key
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: How do you dedicate nodes to one team? → taint the nodes so other Pods stay off, and add a label plus nodeSelector or affinity with a toleration so the team's Pods go there
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: How does the scheduler use taints? → NoSchedule and NoExecute taints filter nodes out; PreferNoSchedule lowers a node's score
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: A Pod is Pending with untolerated taint, what do you do? → read kubectl describe pod events, check the node taints, then add the toleration or remove a stale taint
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: How does kubectl cordon relate to taints? → cordon marks the node unschedulable and adds the node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule taint
title: Taints & Tolerations

text: What are the three tiers? → presentation (frontend), application (backend, often with middleware), and data (database)

text: What does middleware do? → sits between frontend and backend for auth, logging, caching, rate limiting and routing, e.g. an API gateway or message broker

text: Monolith vs microservices? → a monolith is one codebase deployed as one unit; microservices split the app into small services deployed and scaled independently
title: Three-Tier & Microservices

text: Main benefit of microservices? → independent scaling and deployment, plus fault isolation so one failing service doesn't take down the app
title: Three-Tier & Microservices

text: Downside of microservices? → more network calls, more services to deploy and monitor, and harder debugging across service boundaries
title: Three-Tier & Microservices

text: How do microservices map to Kubernetes? → each service gets its own Deployment for its Pods and its own Service for a stable name
title: Three-Tier & Microservices

text: Stateless vs stateful? → stateless keeps no data between requests so any Pod can serve any request; stateful keeps data and needs stable identity and storage
title: Three-Tier & Microservices

text: Why are production databases often kept outside Kubernetes? → stateful workloads need persistent storage, replication, failover and backups, which managed services like RDS handle better

text: What is a StatefulSet? → a controller for stateful apps that gives each Pod a stable name, its own persistent volume and ordered startup
title: Three-Tier & Microservices

text: What is a webhook? → an HTTP callback: a system pushes an event to a URL you registered instead of you polling it, like GitHub notifying Jenkins on a push
title: Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

text: Webhook vs API? → with an API you pull data when you want it; with a webhook the other system pushes data when an event happens
title: Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

text: What are admission controllers? → checks inside the API server, after authentication and authorization and before saving to etcd, that can modify or reject objects

text: Mutating vs validating admission? → mutating can change the object (e.g. inject a sidecar); validating can only allow or deny; mutating runs first

text: Why does order matter? → validation must check the final object, after all mutations
title: Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

text: What happens if an admission webhook is down? → with failurePolicy Fail, matching requests are rejected, which can block Pod creation; scope webhooks narrowly and run them highly available

text: What is a CRD? → a way to extend the Kubernetes API with a new resource type, managed with kubectl like built-in objects
title: Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

text: Does creating a custom resource do anything by itself? → no, it is only stored; a controller must watch and act on it
title: Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

text: What is an operator? → a CRD plus a custom controller that automates running a piece of software, like cert-manager, Argo CD or Prometheus Operator

text: Tools built on admission webhooks? → Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, Istio, cert-manager
title: Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

text: What is Kubernetes? → a declarative container orchestrator; controllers keep reconciling actual state towards the desired state stored in etcd, handling scheduling, self-healing, scaling, service discovery and rollouts
title: Why Kubernetes

text: Why not just Docker? → Docker runs containers on one machine; it has no built-in auto-scaling, multi-host load balancing, self-healing or rolling updates across a cluster
title: Why Kubernetes

text: Declarative vs imperative? → declarative = you describe the end state and the system works out the steps; imperative = you give each step yourself
title: Why Kubernetes

text: What is reconciliation? → the never-ending loop where a controller compares desired and actual state and fixes the difference
title: Why Kubernetes

text: Kubernetes vs Docker Swarm? → Swarm is simpler and built into Docker but has a small ecosystem and basic features; Kubernetes is more complex but is the industry standard with auto-scaling, strong self-healing and a huge ecosystem
title: Why Kubernetes

text: Kubernetes vs ECS? → ECS is simpler and AWS-only; Kubernetes is portable and extensible through CRDs and operators
title: Why Kubernetes

text: Biggest advantage of Kubernetes over competitors? → its extensible API (CRDs + operators), plus portability and the ecosystem
title: Why Kubernetes

text: When would you not use Kubernetes? → small teams with a few services, where ECS or Cloud Run gives the same result with far less operational work
title: Why Kubernetes

text: Imperative vs declarative in Kubernetes? → imperative runs commands that act directly (`kubectl run`, `scale`); declarative describes desired state in a manifest and `kubectl apply` reconciles towards it, idempotently and version-controlled

title: YAML, Manifests & Objects

text: Why is a Pod `v1` but a Deployment `apps/v1`? → Pods are in the unnamed core API group, Deployments are in the apps group; apiVersion is group/version
title: YAML, Manifests & Objects

text: What do alpha, beta and v1 mean? → stability levels; alpha is experimental, beta is mostly stable, v1 is stable; old versions are removed in later releases
title: YAML, Manifests & Objects

title: YAML, Manifests & Objects

title: YAML, Manifests & Objects

title: YAML, Manifests & Objects

text: How does Terraform authenticate to AWS? → the provider uses the standard AWS credential chain: provider config, env vars, shared credentials/config files, then instance or container roles

text: How does Terraform decide creation order? → builds a dependency graph from references; `depends_on` for hidden dependencies

text: What is IaC and why use it? → managing infra through versioned code instead of manual setup; repeatable, reviewable, consistent across environments
title: IaC & Terraform

text: Terraform vs Ansible? → Terraform provisions infrastructure (declarative, stateful), Ansible configures software on machines (procedural, agentless); commonly used together
title: IaC & Terraform

text: Declarative vs imperative? → declarative describes the end state and the tool works out the steps; imperative lists the steps
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What is the Terraform state file? → JSON mapping of resources in code to real objects; used to calculate diffs; may contain secrets, so store it remotely and encrypted
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What does `terraform plan` do? → compares code with state and real infra, shows what would be created, changed or destroyed without changing anything
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What does `-/+` in a plan mean? → the resource will be destroyed and recreated, so check it for data loss
title: IaC & Terraform

text: Is Terraform open source? → not since 2023 (BSL licence); OpenTofu is the open-source fork

text: What is drift? → real infra changed outside Terraform; `plan` detects it and `apply` brings it back to the code

text: What does `prevent_destroy` do? → makes Terraform error on any plan that would destroy the resource

text: Does `prevent_destroy` block replacement? → yes → replacement destroys the old resource

text: What does `ignore_changes` do? → Terraform skips drift on the listed attributes → it also ignores your own config edits to them

title: Lifecycle Rules

text: Variable `validation` vs `precondition`? → `validation` checks one variable, `precondition` can check across variables, data sources and resources
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: When does a postcondition fail without creating anything? → when the attribute is known at plan time
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: What does `replace_triggered_by` do? → replaces a resource when another resource or attribute changes, even if its own arguments did not
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: How do you trigger replacement from a variable change? → put the variable in a `terraform_data` input and reference it in `replace_triggered_by`
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: What is a meta-argument? → an argument available on any resource regardless of provider, e.g. `count`, `for_each`, `depends_on`, `provider`, `lifecycle`
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What is `count.index`? → the zero-based index of the current copy of a resource that uses `count`
title: Meta-Arguments

text: `count` vs `for_each`? → `count` identifies copies by position, `for_each` by key → prefer `for_each` for distinct resources
title: Meta-Arguments

text: Why is `for_each` safer than `count` when removing an item? → with `count` the indexes shift and later resources get destroyed and recreated, with `for_each` only the removed key is touched

title: Meta-Arguments

title: Meta-Arguments

title: Meta-Arguments

text: What is a Terraform provider? → a plugin that implements resources and data sources for an API and translates HCL into API calls

text: Why pin provider versions? → major versions have breaking changes; pinning keeps plans reproducible across machines and CI

title: State & Remote Backend

text: Can you use variables in the backend block? → no, the backend is configured before variables are evaluated; use `-backend-config` for dynamic values
title: State & Remote Backend

text: How do you separate environments? → different state keys (`dev/`, `prod/`) or separate backends, so a change in one can't affect the other

text: `state rm` vs `destroy`? → `state rm` forgets the resource but leaves it running; `destroy` deletes the real resource
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Two engineers apply different code against the same state, what happens? → locking serializes the runs but doesn't merge code; the second plan destroys whatever its code lacks, so use PRs and CI-only applies
title: State & Remote Backend

text: What does `terraform import` do? → adds an existing real resource to state under an address in your code; it writes state only, so the matching resource block must exist first
title: State & Remote Backend

text: How do you bring console-created infra into Terraform? → write matching resource blocks (or use an `import` block with `plan -generate-config-out`), import, then adjust code until `plan` shows no changes
title: State & Remote Backend

text: You renamed a resource in code and the plan wants to recreate it, what do you do? → `terraform state mv <old> <new>` so the existing object is tracked under the new address
title: State & Remote Backend

title: State & Remote Backend

title: Type Constraints

text: `each.key` vs `each.value`? → same for a set; for a map, key is the map key and value is its value
title: Type Constraints

text: Map vs object? → map has any keys with one value type; object has fixed field names with their own types
title: Type Constraints

text: Tuple vs object? → both have a fixed shape with mixed types; tuple by position, object by name; object is more readable and supports `optional()`
title: Type Constraints

text: What does `map(any)` do with `{ a = "x", b = 5 }`? → picks one type for all values, so `5` becomes `"5"`
title: Type Constraints

text: How do you make an object field optional? → `optional(type, default)`, Terraform 1.3+
title: Type Constraints

text: How do you restrict a variable to allowed values? → `validation` block with `contains([...], var.x)` and an `error_message`
title: Type Constraints

text: What's the most common real-world `for_each` type? → `map(object({...}))`: many items, each with the same shape
title: Type Constraints

text: Does `terraform validate` catch a wrong value like a region in `instance_type`? → no, it checks syntax and types only; the AWS API rejects it at `apply`
title: Type Constraints

text: Variable vs local? → a variable is an input set from outside per run; a local is a value computed inside the module and can't be overridden
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: Why can't a variable's default use another variable? → defaults must be fixed values; computed values belong in locals
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: What is the variable precedence order? → default, then `TF_VAR_` env vars, `terraform.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json`, `*.auto.tfvars` in alphabetical order, and `-var` / `-var-file` on the command line last and strongest
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: `terraform.tfvars` vs `prod.tfvars`? → `terraform.tfvars` and `*.auto.tfvars` load automatically; any other name loads only with `-var-file`
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: How do you pass secrets to Terraform? → `TF_VAR_` env vars or a secrets manager, mark the variable `sensitive = true`; the value still lands in state, so the state must be protected
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: How do you enforce common tags on all resources? → a `common_tags` local merged into each resource's tags with `merge()`, or the AWS provider's `default_tags` block
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: list vs set vs tuple? → list is ordered with duplicates, set is unordered and unique, tuple has a fixed length with a type per position
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: map vs object? → map has any keys with one value type; object has fixed keys with their own types
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: What are outputs used for? → showing values after apply, feeding scripts via `-raw` / `-json`, and passing values between modules and stacks
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: Does `sensitive = true` hide a value from state? → no, only from CLI output
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: How do you get unique S3 bucket names? → add a suffix from `random_string` (stored in state so it stays stable) or include account and region in the name
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: Is changing a variable enough to create a separate prod environment? → no, with the same backend key it modifies the same resources; prod needs its own state
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs
